lead: Torque is crankshaft twist. Power is torque × angular speed. BSFC is fuel mass to deliver each kWh at the crankshaft, in g/kWh. A large slow engine has big torque and modest power; a small fast engine reverses this. A badly matched engine can be thirsty at both low and high speed.
prereq: You need the rich-mixture torque/fuel trade-off from 4.2 and work, power and energy basics.

blocks.text: Torque T is crankshaft twisting effort, in N·m. A dynamometer holds speed steady and measures it. Turning the shaft one radian delivers T joule, so shaft power is T × ω, where ω is angular speed in rad/s.

blocks.where: P is brake power in W; T is brake torque in N·m; N is speed in rev/min; 2π/60 converts rev/min to rad/s.

blocks.text: Brake power is power left at the crankshaft after friction and pumping losses. At 3000 rpm and 150 N·m, P = 2π×3000×150÷60 = 47.1 kW. At 4000 rpm torque is 145 N·m but P = 60.7 kW. Speed multiplies torque; beyond the torque peak speed still rises faster than torque falls, so power climbs.

BMEP is brake work per cycle divided by swept volume of all cylinders. For a four-stroke, BMEP = 4πT ÷ V_d; for a two-stroke, BMEP = 2πT ÷ V_d. T is N·m, V_d is m³, BMEP is Pa. T ÷ V_d is only proportional to BMEP, but that is enough to compare engines of different sizes.
A fuel flow meter gives fuel mass flow ṁ_f, usually kg/h. BSFC is that flow divided by brake power.

blocks.where: BSFC is in g/kWh; ṁ_f is in kg/h; P is in kW; 1000 converts kg to g.

blocks.text: Small BSFC is good. Petrol engines reach about 240–260 g/kWh at best point. Diesels reach 200 g/kWh or below because higher compression extracts more work.
One kWh delivered is 3600 kJ. Fuel burnt to make it holds BSFC × CV kilojoule, where CV is calorific value.

blocks.where: η_bth is a fraction; BSFC is in g/kWh; CV is in MJ/kg (= kJ/g); 3600 is kJ per kWh.

blocks.text: At 244.04 g/kWh and 43 MJ/kg, η_bth = 3600 ÷ 10 494 = 0.3431, or 34.3 percent. About two-thirds leaves as heat.

sections.h3: The BSFC map and mechanical efficiency

blocks.text: A BSFC map plots contours of BSFC against speed (x) and brake torque or load (y). Its low-BSFC island sits at moderate speed, about 2000–3000 rpm, and high load near wide-open throttle.

items: Friction and pumping grow with speed, so at high rpm more fuel just turns the engine.
At light load fixed losses are shared over little brake power, so BSFC is poor.
At full load enrichment protects components, and extra fuel raises BSFC again (see 4.2).

blocks.text: Indicated power is gas power inside cylinders. Brake power survives after friction and pumping. Friction power = indicated − brake. Mechanical efficiency η_m = P_brake ÷ P_indicated; petrol engines run about 0.85, falling at high speed.
These variables set the ECU fuel and spark tables in 4.4.

figure.caption: Torque peaks at 150 N·m at 3000 rpm; power keeps rising to about 69 kW at 6000 rpm because speed multiplies torque.

spec.aria: Torque peaks at 150 N·m at 3000 rpm and falls away, while power keeps climbing to about 69 kW at 6000 rpm because it is torque multiplied by speed.

examples.question: A four-cylinder petrol engine runs at 3000 rev/min and 150 N·m. Fuel flow is 11.5 kg/h; petrol CV is 43 MJ/kg. Find brake power, BSFC and brake thermal efficiency.
examples.check:
import math
N = 3000.0
T = 150.0
P = 2*math.pi*N*T/60.0
P_kW = P/1000.0
m_dot_kg_h = 11.5
bsfc = m_dot_kg_h*1000.0/P_kW
CV = 43.0
eta_pct = 3600.0/(bsfc*CV)*100.0
print(round(P_kW, 2))
print(round(bsfc, 2))
print(round(eta_pct, 2))

traps: Putting rev/min straight into P = Tω; convert with ω = 2πN/60.
Forgetting 1000 in BSFC; kg/h ÷ kW gives kg/kWh, 1000 times too small.
Confusing torque peak with power peak; power peaks at higher speed.
Wrong CV unit in η = 3600/(BSFC×CV); use MJ/kg (= kJ/g).

quiz.q: Define BSFC and give its unit.
quiz.a: Fuel mass flow ÷ brake power, in g/kWh.

quiz.q: Write the relation between brake power, torque and speed, naming every symbol and unit.
quiz.a: P = 2πNT/60; P in W, T in N·m, N in rev/min.

quiz.q: Torque peaks at 3000 rpm but power peaks near 6000 rpm. Explain why.
quiz.a: Power = torque × speed. Past the torque peak speed still rises faster than torque falls, so the product grows until the torque fall wins.

quiz.q: An engine holds 130 N·m at 2500 rev/min. Find the brake power.
A diesel uses 9 kg/h of fuel while delivering 40 kW of brake power. CV is 43 MJ/kg. Find BSFC and brake thermal efficiency.
Why does the lowest-BSFC island sit at moderate speed and high load rather than at maximum speed and full throttle?
quiz.a: High speed: friction and pumping grow. Light load: fixed losses are shared over little power. Full load: enrichment adds fuel for little extra work.

quiz.q: Brake power is 60 kW and mechanical efficiency is 0.85. Find indicated power and friction power.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the BSFC map is stored as ECU breakpoint tables of speed against load; calibration moves breakpoints to cover the driving cycle. Hybrid controllers choose brake power inside the island and let the battery carry peaks.
